name: 19-Nor-4-androstenedione (19-norandrostenedione)

card.summary: A nandrolone prohormone from the supplement era, now mostly a doping-control footnote.
card.note: Controlled in the US; prohibited in sport; can cause positive nandrolone tests.

quick.overview:
19-Norandrostenedione is a prohormone that converts to nandrolone. It was sold as a supplement in the US until 2005.

Research on it centres on doping tests rather than muscle outcomes.
quick.mechanism: After oral intake it converts to nandrolone and shares its urinary metabolite.
quick.risks: US Schedule III, banned in sport. Contaminated supplements have caused positive nandrolone tests.

lead: 19-Nor-4-androstenedione, also called 19-norandrostenedione or bolandione, is a steroid that is a precursor of nandrolone. It was sold over the counter in the US as a prohormone supplement until 2005.[2] Prohormone products were marketed to people who wanted to build muscle, and a larger, leaner physique is the appearance goal behind them: the idea was that the body would convert the precursor into nandrolone and so raise anabolic signalling.[1][2][6]

It is best documented in the literature through doping research. A 2000 JAMA study found trace contamination of over-the-counter androstenedione products and examined whether androstenedione and 19-norandrostenedione ingestion causes positive urine tests for a nandrolone metabolite.[1] Today it is a controlled substance in the US and is prohibited in sport.[2]

Researchers have also looked at where the compound comes from in nature. 19-Norandrostenedione has been identified in human, porcine and equine ovarian and testicular fluids and in the early equine conceptus, which is why anti-doping scientists treat small urinary amounts of its metabolites with care.[3][14][15][16]

chain: Converted in the body to nandrolone
angle.text: Supplement-era marketing presented 19-norandrostenedione as a way to build muscle by supplying a nandrolone precursor. Reviews of the 'andro' prohormone class describe the muscle and strength claims as contradicted by most studies.

paras: Taken orally, it converts readily to nandrolone, and it activates the androgen receptor about ten times less strongly than dihydrotestosterone.[2] In castrated rats it increased levator ani muscle weight without changing prostate or seminal vesicle weight, which the Wikipedia article reads as selective muscle effects with weak androgenic activity; a rat study also found oral dosing a poor route for building skeletal muscle and capable of causing side effects.[2]

It is a 19-nor steroid like those found naturally in small quantities, for example in human ovarian follicular fluid, where 19-norandrostenedione and 19-nortestosterone have been measured.[3] A review of endogenous androgens notes that nandrolone and 19-norandrostenedione are produced endogenously, with minor by-products of androgen aromatization an appealing hypothesis.[5] In cultured breast tissue experiments, 19-norandrostenedione at a micromolar concentration reduced estrone formation by about 80 percent, showing it can interact with aromatase.[7]

One reported synthetic route starts from estrone methyl ether, reduces it to nandrolone and reoxidises it at the 17-position; the compound is also an intermediate in making steroids such as norethandrolone and norethindrone.[2]

sections.h: Effectiveness and safety of andro prohormones
paras: A 2003 review of the 'andro' prohormones, a group that includes androstenedione, 4-androstenediol, 5-androstenediol, 19-norandrostenediol and 19-norandrostenedione, reported that manufacturers claimed they raise testosterone, strength and muscle mass, reduce body fat, and improve mood and sexual performance. The review stated that most studies contradict these claims, and that several studies of oral andro prohormones showed abnormal rises in oestrogen-related hormones and falls in HDL cholesterol, which it linked to cardiovascular and cancer risk markers.[4] A randomised trial of multiple oral doses of androgenic anabolic steroids measured endurance performance and indices of physical stress in healthy men, as part of the wider research on these agents.[8]

Because it and nandrolone share the urinary metabolite 19-norandrosterone, contaminated supplements can yield positive tests.[1][2] A 2010 randomised trial gave 19 volunteers 10 micrograms of 19-norandrostenedione in water or in an energy bar and found that the supplement matrix affected excretion of the metabolites.[9] The norethisterone contraceptive, which can carry a 19-norandrostenedione impurity, was found to produce urinary 19-norandrosterone above the 2 ng/mL reporting threshold in female volunteers.[10] A registered phase 1/2 trial (started 2006, 20 participants) studied the risk of positive doping tests after ingesting supplements contaminated with trace nandrolone metabolites.[11]

Anti-doping laboratories identify nandrolone use by measuring 19-norandrosterone in urine, and 19-norandrostenedione is one of several routes that lead to it. A 2009 pair of studies from the UK examined norethisterone, a progestogen used for menstrual disorders and contraception that sometimes contains 19-norandrostenedione as a tablet impurity. In ten female volunteers taking norethisterone at doses used for menstrual disorders, peak urinary 19-norandrosterone reached roughly 51 to 63 ng/mL, far above the 2 ng/mL laboratory reporting threshold, whether or not the tablet carried the impurity; a single 1 microgram dose of 19-norandrostenedione produced a peak of about 2.4 ng/mL.[10][17] The authors concluded that the drug itself, rather than the impurity, accounted for most of the signal.[10]

In the 2010 randomised crossover study, 19 volunteers (10 men and 9 women, average age 26) swallowed 10 micrograms of 19-norandrostenedione either in 500 mL of water or in an energy bar. Average peak urinary 19-norandrosterone was about 4.8 ng/mL after water and about 8.5 ng/mL after the bar, and total urine volume differed between the two conditions, indicating that the food matrix changes how the metabolite appears in urine.[9]

A 2007 doping-control study tested what happens when 19-norandrostenedione is taken together with finasteride, a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor. Finasteride reduced urinary 19-norandrosterone by up to 84 percent in elimination studies and shifted several routinely monitored steroid-profile markers, which the authors described as a complication for testing.[18] The finding is relevant to people who use finasteride for hair and also train, because the drug appears on the WADA prohibited list for this masking potential.

19-Norandrostenedione is not purely synthetic. It was measured for the first time in human preovulatory follicular fluid in 1987, where its level correlated with estradiol, and has since been found in porcine follicular fluid, equine testes and the yolk-sac fluid of the early horse conceptus.[3][15][16][14] Researchers have proposed that it arises as a minor by-product of aromatase acting on androgens, and equine placental synthesis from DHEA is inhibited by aromatase inhibitors.[5][19] These findings are part of why laboratories set reporting thresholds rather than treating any detection as proof of administration.

sections.h: Prohormone era in looksmaxxing and bodybuilding
paras: During the late 1990s and early 2000s, over-the-counter prohormone supplements were a standard topic in bodybuilding magazines and forums as a route to a larger physique. T Nation threads from the period show users trading label chemical names and discussing mixed formulas containing androstenedione and 19-norandrostenedione, and a long 2008 reference thread catalogued prohormone nomenclature.[12][13][20] The 2004 Anabolic Steroid Control Act and a 2005 rule ended open sales in the US, and the community focus then moved to other compounds.[2][6]

The 2000 JAMA randomised study assessed the purity of over-the-counter androstenedione and whether administration of androstenedione or 19-norandrostenedione leads to positive tests for a nandrolone metabolite.[1] The 2010 trial in 19 volunteers (10 men, 9 women) and the 2006 registered study concerned urinary excretion and doping tests, not muscle or appearance outcomes.[9][11] No trials have evaluated muscle or appearance outcomes of 19-norandrostenedione.

Prohormone supplements were popular from about 1960 to 2001 in a largely unregulated market, including in professional baseball; the US Anabolic Steroid Control Act of 2004 banned androstenedione and androstenediol, and some banned prohormones later reappeared under new chemical names.[6] 19-Norandrostenedione itself was sold over the counter in the US until 2005 and is now Schedule III and prohibited in sport.[2] On T Nation, a 2004 thread titled 'FDA to Ban Andro!' quoted draft legislation listing 19-nor-4-androstenedione, and prohormone forum threads from 2008 discuss the products' chemical names and mixtures.[12][13]

timeline.event: 19-Norandrostenedione and 19-nortestosterone measured for the first time in human follicular fluid.[3]
JAMA study on trace contamination and nandrolone-metabolite positives.[1]
Anabolic Steroid Control Act bans androstenedione and androstenediol in the US.[6]

lore.intro: Forum discussion of 19-norandrostenedione is mostly historical, from the era when prohormones were legal supplements.[12][13]

claims.claim: Prohormones convert to nandrolone and build muscle like a steroid
claims.believers: Mid-2000s forum posts describe prohormone stacks containing androstenedione and 19-norandrostenedione as muscle-building supplements.[13]
claims.experts: A 2003 review concluded that most studies contradict muscle and strength claims for andro prohormones and reported oestrogen and lipid changes.[4]

claims.claim: The compound was banned because it works
claims.believers: Forum users in 2004 discussed legislation listing 19-nor-4-androstenedione among banned prohormones.[12]
claims.experts: Regulators placed it in Schedule III and it is prohibited by WADA; contamination of other supplements with it also produced positive nandrolone tests.[1][2]

claims.claim: A trace of 19-nor prohormone in a supplement can trigger a positive drug test
claims.believers: Athletes and forum users have argued that contaminated or over-the-counter supplements explain unexpected nandrolone findings.[12]
claims.experts: The 2000 JAMA study and later excretion trials show that small ingested amounts of 19-norandrostenedione can yield urinary 19-norandrosterone, and the 2009 norethisterone work shows other drugs can do the same.[1][9][10]
